summary.text: A 65-year-old woman presented after six months of progressive tiredness, loss of appetite and weight loss with new-onset mild confusion. History included multiple sclerosis, hypertension, osteoarthritis and hiatus hernia; she lived alone, did not smoke, abstained from alcohol and had a chronically poor appetite. A GP visit three months before admission had led to folic acid 5 mg daily for two months.

She was markedly pale and jaundiced, without lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or neurological features of B12 deficiency. Investigations showed profound pancytopenia, macrocytosis, megaloblastic blood film, raised bilirubin and LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, vitamin B12 114 ng/L and folate 1.4 µg/L; CT head and abdomen-pelvis excluded acute intracranial and malignant causes, and bone marrow biopsy confirmed megaloblastic change.

She received transfusions, hydroxocobalamin 1 mg intramuscularly on alternate days, oral folic acid 5 mg daily, filgrastim and prednisolone; oral maintenance therapy followed parenteral repletion. Counts recovered within about two weeks, haemoglobin dipped to 89 g/L on day 25 with iron deficiency corrected by intravenous iron, and she was discharged and remains well on follow-up.
